title: Linear Equations in One Variable, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we learned that a linear equation in one variable has a single unknown number. Our job is to undo operations until that unknown stands alone.
The key rule is balance. Whatever we do to one side of the equation, we must do to the other side, so that both sides stay equal.

card.text: Do the same to both sides

beats.say: In this video, we apply these ideas to two harder problems. First a medium one with fractions, then a hard one that looks like a real SAT question.
Here's a medium problem. x over four plus x over six equals ten. Fractions make the arithmetic messy, so our first move will be to remove them.
The denominators are four and six. The smallest number that both divide into evenly is twelve, called the least common denominator. Multiplying by twelve will clear both fractions.
Multiply every single term on both sides by twelve, including the ten. Twelve times x over four is three x. Twelve times x over six is two x. Twelve times ten is one hundred twenty.
Now combine the like terms on the left. Three x plus two x is five x, so the equation becomes five x equals one hundred twenty.
Divide both sides by five to get x alone. One hundred twenty divided by five is twenty-four. So x equals twenty-four.
Check by substituting twenty-four into the original equation. Twenty-four divided by four is six, and twenty-four divided by six is four. Six plus four is ten, which matches the right side.
Now a hard problem, in the style of the SAT. One half times the quantity eight x minus six, plus k x, equals three minus two x. The number k is a constant, and the equation has no solution. Find k.
Before solving, we make a plan. We'll simplify both sides into the form a x plus b equals c x plus d. Then we use what that form tells us about the number of solutions.
First distribute the one half to both terms inside the parentheses. One half of eight x is four x, and one half of negative six is negative three.
Next, group the two x terms on the left. Four x plus k x is the quantity four plus k, times x. Now both sides have the form a x plus b.
No solution means the x coefficients are equal while the constants are different. So we set four plus k equal to negative two, which is the coefficient on the right side.
Subtract four from both sides. Negative two minus four is negative six, so k equals negative six.

Always verify. With k equal to negative six, the equation becomes negative two x minus three equals negative two x plus three. The x terms cancel and leave negative three equals three, which is never true.
This table summarizes the rule we just used. After simplifying to a x plus b equals c x plus d, we compare the coefficients and constants. If a and c are different, there's exactly one solution.
If a equals c but b and d are different, both sides have the same slope but different intercepts, so they never meet. There's no solution. This is our problem.
If a equals c and b equals d, the two sides are identical. Every value of x works, so there are infinitely many solutions.
Desmos gives us a way to see the answer. We'll graph each side of the equation as its own line, and let a slider control the unknown constant k.
Type the left side as y equals one half times the quantity eight x minus six, plus k x. Desmos notices the new letter k and offers a slider for it.
Now type the right side as a second line, y equals three minus two x. Both sides of the equation are now graphed, and an intersection would be a solution.
Drag the slider for k and watch the first line. As k decreases, the line rotates. When k reaches negative six, the lines become parallel. They never cross, which means no solution.
Parallel lines that never meet confirm our algebra. The value of k that gives no solution is negative six.
To recap. To clear fractions, multiply every term by the least common denominator. Remember to multiply the whole numbers too.
beats.item: Clear fractions with the common denominator

beats.say: Distribute first, then group the x terms so the equation looks like a x plus b equals c x plus d.
beats.item: Distribute, then group the x terms

beats.say: Compare the coefficients and constants to decide between one solution, no solution, or infinitely many. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way with Desmos.
